pairs.source_text: huic nomen graece Onagost fabulae; Demophilus scripsit, Maccus vortit barbare; Asinariam volt esse, si per vos licet.
pairs.question: Quod nomen Graecum habebat fabula ex qua Plautus Asinariam suam fecit?
pairs.question_en: What Greek title did the play have from which Plautus made his Asinaria?
pairs.derivation: The prologue names the Greek original: Onagos ('the ass-driver'), which Plautus turned into the Asinaria. Anchored to Plautus + Asinaria; one-word title answer stated verbatim (Onagost = Onagos est). A famous authorship fact.

pairs.source_text: Demophilus scripsit, Maccus vortit barbare; Asinariam volt esse, si per vos licet.
pairs.question: Quis poeta Graecus fabulam scripsit quam Plautus in Asinariam vertit, ut prologus narrat?
pairs.question_en: Which Greek poet wrote the play that Plautus turned into the Asinaria, as the prologue relates?
pairs.derivation: The prologue credits the Greek source-play to Demophilus (Demophilus scripsit). Anchored to Asinaria + Plautus; one-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Demophilus scripsit, Maccus vortit barbare; Asinariam volt esse, si per vos licet.
pairs.question: Quo nomine se ipse auctor in prologo Asinariae appellat, qui fabulam Demophili barbare vertit?
pairs.question_en: By what name does the author call himself in the prologue of the Asinaria, the one who turned Demophilus' play into Latin?
pairs.derivation: A celebrated authorship fact: in the Asinaria prologue Plautus names himself 'Maccus' (Maccus vortit barbare). Anchored to the named play + prologue; one-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: huic nomen graece Onagost fabulae; Demophilus scripsit, Maccus vortit barbare; Asinariam volt esse, si per vos licet.
pairs.question: Quod nomen Latinum Plautus fabulae imponere vult, quae graece Onagos inscribebatur?
pairs.question_en: What Latin title does Plautus wish to give the play that in Greek was called Onagos?
pairs.derivation: The prologue gives the Latin title (Asinariam volt esse). Anchored to Plautus + the Greek Onagos; one-word title answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Demophilus scripsit, Maccus vortit barbare; Asinariam volt esse, si per vos licet.
pairs.question: In quam linguam Plautus se fabulam Demophili 'vortisse' dicit, quam more Graeco 'barbaram' vocat?
pairs.question_en: Into what language does Plautus say he 'turned' Demophilus' play, which in the Greek manner he calls 'barbarian'?
pairs.derivation: 'Maccus vortit barbare' — Plautus rendered the Greek original into Latin, which Greeks (and Plautus jokingly) call the 'barbarian' tongue. Anchored to Plautus + Demophilus; short answer; the fact (translation into Latin) is standard.

pairs.source_text: dotalem servom Sauream uxor tua adduxit, cui plus in manu sit quam tibi.
pairs.question: Quis servus dotalis, ab uxore Demaeneti in domum adductus, plus in manu quam ipse dominus habet apud Plautum in Asinaria?
pairs.question_en: What dowry-slave, brought into the house by Demaenetus' wife, holds more in his control than the master himself, in Plautus' Asinaria?
pairs.derivation: Roman realia of the dotata uxor: the wife's dowry included a slave, Saurea, who as dotalis controls more of the household money than Demaenetus. Anchored to Demaenetus + Asinaria; one-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Argentum accepi, dote imperium vendidi.
pairs.question: Quid Demaenetus se pro dote uxoris accepta vendidisse apud Plautum in Asinaria dicit?
pairs.question_en: What does Demaenetus say he sold in return for accepting his wife's dowry, in Plautus' Asinaria?
pairs.derivation: The henpecked-husband/dotata-uxor theme compressed into a line: by taking the dowry Demaenetus 'sold his authority.' Anchored to Demaenetus + Asinaria; short answer verbatim (dote imperium vendidi).

pairs.source_text: dic, quid me aequom censes pro illa tibi dare, annum hunc ne cum quiquam alio sit? CLEAR. Tene? viginti minas;
pairs.question: Quot minas Cleareta lena ab Argyrippo poscit, ut Philaenium annum unum cum nullo alio sit, apud Plautum in Asinaria?
pairs.question_en: How many minae does the bawd Cleareta demand from Argyrippus, so that Philaenium be with no other man for a year, in Plautus' Asinaria?
pairs.derivation: The sum that drives the plot: twenty minae for a year's exclusive claim to Philaenium. Anchored to Cleareta + Argyrippus + Asinaria; number answer verbatim (viginti minas).

pairs.source_text: Non tu scis? hic noster quaestus aucupi simillimust.
pairs.question: Cui arti Cleareta lena quaestum suum lenonium simillimum esse dicit apud Plautum in Asinaria?
pairs.question_en: To what craft does the bawd Cleareta say her trade as a procuress is most similar, in Plautus' Asinaria?
pairs.derivation: Cleareta's set-piece on the courtesan-house economics: the bawd's trade works like fowling (bait the field, the lovers are the birds). Anchored to Cleareta + Asinaria; one-word answer verbatim (aucupi simillimust).

pairs.source_text: portitorum simillumae sunt ianuae lenoniae: si adfers, tum patent, si non est quod des, aedes non patent.
pairs.question: Quibus Cleareta lena ianuas domus lenoniae similes esse dicit, quae adferenti pecuniam patent, non habenti clausae sunt, apud Plautum in Asinaria?
pairs.question_en: To whom does the bawd Cleareta liken the doors of a procuress' house, which open to one who brings money and stay shut to one who has none, in Plautus' Asinaria?
pairs.derivation: A mercenary maxim of the trade: the doors of the bawd's house are like the portitores (customs-men), open only to those who pay. Anchored to Cleareta + Asinaria; one-word answer verbatim (portitorum simillumae).

pairs.source_text: quasi piscis, itidemst amator lenae: nequam est, nisi recens;
pairs.question: Cui animali Cleareta lena amatorem comparat, quem 'nequam esse nisi recentem' ait apud Plautum in Asinaria?
pairs.question_en: To what creature does the bawd Cleareta compare a lover, saying he is 'no good unless fresh,' in Plautus' Asinaria?
pairs.derivation: Cleareta's simile on the trade: a lover is like a fish, worthless unless fresh (still paying). Anchored to Cleareta + Asinaria; one-word answer verbatim (quasi piscis).

pairs.source_text: meministin asinos Arcadicos mercatori Pellaeo nostrum vendere atriensem?
pairs.question: Ex venditione quorum animalium ortum est illud argentum quod servi Libanus et Leonida in Asinaria Plauti intercipiunt?
pairs.question_en: From the sale of which animals arose the money that the slaves Libanus and Leonida intercept in Plautus' Asinaria?
pairs.answer_en: From the sale of Arcadian asses (donkeys).
pairs.derivation: The title-fact: the plot turns on the price of asses. Demaenetus' steward had sold Arcadian asses, and the returned price (twenty minae) is intercepted by the slaves. Anchored to the named play + slaves; supported verbatim (asinos Arcadicos ... vendere atriensem).

pairs.source_text: meministin asinos Arcadicos mercatori Pellaeo nostrum vendere atriensem?
pairs.question: Cui mercatori atriensis Demaeneti asinos Arcadicos vendiderat, cuius pretium in Asinaria Plauti intercipitur?
pairs.question_en: To what merchant had Demaenetus' steward sold the Arcadian asses, whose price is intercepted in Plautus' Asinaria?
pairs.derivation: The buyer of the asses was a Pellaean merchant (mercator Pellaeus), whose agent brings the price. Anchored to Demaenetus + Asinaria; short answer verbatim (mercatori Pellaeo).

pairs.source_text: Ait se ob asinos ferre argentum atriensi Saureae, viginti minas, sed eum sese non nosse hominem qui siet, ipsum vero se novisse callide Demaenetum.
pairs.question: Quod officium in domo Demaeneti servus Saurea gerit, cui pretium asinorum dandum erat apud Plautum in Asinaria?
pairs.question_en: What office does the slave Saurea hold in Demaenetus' household, to whom the price of the asses was to be paid, in Plautus' Asinaria?
pairs.derivation: Roman household realia: Saurea is the atriensis, the chief house-steward, to whom the ass-money is owed. Anchored to Saurea + Demaenetus + Asinaria; one-word office answer verbatim (atriensi Saureae).

pairs.source_text: te ex Leonida futurum esse atriensem Sauream, dum argentum afferat mercator pro asinis.
pairs.question: Cuius personam servus Leonida induit, ut argentum pro asinis solvendum intercipiat, apud Plautum in Asinaria?
pairs.question_en: Whose identity does the slave Leonida assume, in order to intercept the money to be paid for the asses, in Plautus' Asinaria?
pairs.derivation: The central con of the play: Leonida pretends to be the steward Saurea to receive the ass-money from the merchant's agent. Anchored to Leonida + Asinaria; short answer verbatim (te ex Leonida futurum esse atriensem Sauream).

pairs.source_text: lupus est homo homini, non homo, quom qualis sit non novit.
pairs.question: Quid homo homini esse, non homo, apud Plautum in Asinaria dicitur, dum qualis alter sit ignoratur?
pairs.question_en: According to Plautus in the Asinaria, what is a man to a man — not a man — so long as he does not know what sort the other is?
pairs.derivation: The origin of the proverb 'homo homini lupus': in the Asinaria the wary merchant says a man is a wolf to a stranger he does not know. Anchored to the named play; one-word answer verbatim (lupus est homo homini).

pairs.source_text: nemo etiam me accusavit merito meo, neque me alter est Athenis hodie quisquam, cui credi recte aeque putent.
pairs.question: In qua urbe fabula Plauti Asinaria agitur, ut Leonida servus indicat?
pairs.question_en: In what city is Plautus' play Asinaria set, as the slave Leonida indicates?
pairs.derivation: The setting: Leonida boasts that no one in Athens is held more trustworthy, placing the action there. Anchored to the named play; one-word place answer verbatim (Athenis).

pairs.source_text: Etiam opilio qui pascit, mater, alienas ovis, aliquam habet peculiarem, qui spem soletur suam.
pairs.question: Cuius operis exemplo Philaenium utitur, ut sibi unum amatorem proprium habere liceat, apud Plautum in Asinaria?
pairs.question_en: By the example of which worker does Philaenium argue that she may keep one lover of her own, in Plautus' Asinaria?
pairs.derivation: Philaenium's proverb: even the shepherd tending another's flock keeps one sheep of his own (peculiaris), so she may keep one lover. Anchored to Philaenium + Asinaria; one-word answer verbatim (opilio qui pascit ... alienas ovis).

pairs.source_text: argenti viginti minae me ad mortem appulerunt, quas hodie adulescens Diabolus ipsi daturus dixit, ut hanc ne quoquam mitteret nisi ad se hunc annum totum.
pairs.question: Quis adulescens Argyrippo de Philaenio amanda rivalis est apud Plautum in Asinaria?
pairs.question_en: What young man is Argyrippus' rival for the love of Philaenium in Plautus' Asinaria?
pairs.derivation: The rival lover: Diabolus offers the lena twenty minae for a year's exclusive claim to Philaenium, threatening to outbid Argyrippus. Anchored to Argyrippus + Philaenium + Asinaria; one-name answer verbatim (adulescens Diabolus).

pairs.source_text: Diabolus Glauci filius Clearetae lenae dedit dono argenti viginti minas, Philaenium ut secum esset noctes et dies hunc annum totum.
pairs.question: Cuius filius est Diabolus, rivalis Argyrippi, ut in syngrapho Asinariae Plauti scribitur?
pairs.question_en: Whose son is Diabolus, Argyrippus' rival, as written in the contract of Plautus' Asinaria?
pairs.derivation: The contract opens by naming the parties: 'Diabolus, son of Glaucus.' Name-relation fact anchored to Diabolus + Asinaria; one-name answer verbatim (Diabolus Glauci filius).

pairs.source_text: Agedum istum ostende quem conscripsti syngraphum inter me et amicam et lenam. leges pellege.
pairs.question: Quo nomine appellatur illud pactum scriptum quod Diabolus cum lena Cleareta de Philaenio init apud Plautum in Asinaria?
pairs.question_en: By what name is the written contract called that Diabolus makes with the bawd Cleareta over Philaenium in Plautus' Asinaria?
pairs.derivation: Roman contract realia parodied: the lovers' agreement is drawn up as a formal syngraphus (written bond) with clauses read out like a statute. Anchored to Diabolus + Cleareta + Asinaria; one-word answer verbatim (syngraphum ... conscripsti).

pairs.source_text: Neque ullum verbum faciat perplexabile, neque ulla lingua sciat loqui nisi Attica.
pairs.question: Qua sola lingua Philaenium loqui, ex syngrapho Diaboli, apud Plautum in Asinaria licet?
pairs.question_en: According to Diabolus' contract in the Asinaria, in what language alone is Philaenium permitted to speak?
pairs.derivation: A clause of the jealous contract: Philaenium may know no tongue but Attic, reflecting the trope of the refined courtesan speaking pure Attic Greek. Anchored to Diabolus' syngraphus + Asinaria; one-word answer verbatim (nisi Attica).

pairs.source_text: nam me hodie oravit Argyrippus filius, uti sibi amanti facerem argenti copiam;
pairs.question: Cui, contra uxorem suam, Demaenetus senex argenti copiam ad amorem faciendam parat apud Plautum in Asinaria?
pairs.question_en: For whom, against his own wife, does the old man Demaenetus arrange a supply of money for love, in Plautus' Asinaria?
pairs.derivation: The driving premise: the henpecked Demaenetus conspires against his wife to help his lovesick son Argyrippus find the money for the courtesan. Anchored to Demaenetus + Asinaria; one-name answer verbatim (oravit Argyrippus filius ... facerem argenti copiam).

pairs.source_text: Iace, pater, talos, ut porro nos iaciamus. DEM. Maxime. te, Philaenium, mihi atque uxoris mortem. hoc Venerium est.
pairs.question: Quo nomine Demaenetus optimum talorum iactum appellat, cum in Asinaria Plauti talos iacit?
pairs.question_en: By what name does Demaenetus call the best throw of the knucklebones when he casts the dice in Plautus' Asinaria?
pairs.derivation: Roman gaming realia: the highest cast of the tali was the 'Venus' throw. Demaenetus names his winning cast 'Venerium.' Anchored to Demaenetus + Asinaria; one-word answer verbatim (hoc Venerium est).

pairs.source_text: sine, revenias modo domum, faxo ut scias quid pericli sit dotatae uxori vitium dicere.
pairs.question: Cuius generis uxori Demaenetum, ut Artemona minatur, periculose vitium dicere apud Plautum in Asinaria docetur?
pairs.question_en: What kind of wife does Demaenetus dangerously insult, as Artemona threatens, in Plautus' Asinaria?
pairs.derivation: The dotata-uxor theme made explicit: the wife who brought a dowry holds power, and it is perilous to insult her. Anchored to Demaenetus/Artemona + Asinaria; verbatim (dotatae uxori vitium dicere).

pairs.source_text: Cano capite te cuculum uxor ex lustris rapit.
pairs.question: Vnde uxor Artemona Demaenetum maritum canum in fine Asinariae Plauti domum abstrahit?
pairs.question_en: From where does his wife Artemona drag the grey-haired husband Demaenetus home at the end of Plautus' Asinaria?
pairs.derivation: The play's punchline: the dotata wife Artemona catches Demaenetus feasting with his son's mistress and hauls him home from the lustra. Anchored to Demaenetus + Artemona + Asinaria; short answer verbatim (ex lustris rapit). Artemona is named in the dialogue (line 855).
